clue.text: Stage managers with New Order leaving en masse for Pulp's 'Common People'

definitions.note: the riff-raff, the rabble; also the title of the Pulp hit

indicators.note: the band's name doubles as a call for a fresh arrangement of the letters of stage managers
the letters of en masse depart from that pool, leaving the rest to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A music-press note: stage crew and the band New Order mingling at a gig by Pulp, whose hit was 'Common People'.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: take the letters of STAGE MANAGERS, strike out those of EN MASSE, and rearrange the six left over (T, G, A, G, R, A). Pulp and New Order are both British bands.
explanation.definitionFit: Ragtag, as in 'ragtag and bobtail', is a dismissive term for the rabble, the ordinary masses.

clue.text: Strangely, this spirit's bottled

indicators.note: the spirit is kept bottled up within the single word Strangely

explanation.surface: A puzzled drinker notes that, oddly, this spirit has been bottled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' and 'bottled' suggest liquor, but the spirit is a heavenly one, held within the letters of 'Strangely'.
explanation.definitionFit: An angel is a heavenly spirit, a supernatural messenger in religious tradition.

clue.text: Spooner having offered £25, Miss Daisy riots here

definitions.note: the place where riots happened: a Welsh mining town famous for its 1910 riots

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner's habit of swapping the opening sounds of two words is applied to the pair that follows

parts.note: pony is British slang for twenty-five pounds
Jessica Tandy played the title role in the film Driving Miss Daisy

explanation.surface: An odd scene: Spooner offering twenty-five pounds while Miss Daisy riots.
explanation.walkthrough: PONY TANDY with the first letters swapped gives TONY PANDY. In Britain a 'pony' is £25 in slang. Tonypandy is a town in the Rhondda valley, South Wales, where striking miners rioted in 1910.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonypandy is the Rhondda mining town remembered for the 1910 riots during a coal strike.

clue.text: Good — it's jettisoned by arrogant swimmer

indicators.note: thrown overboard from the word for arrogant, so those letters are removed

parts.note: uppity means self-important or arrogant
the word it, with 's standing for is as a link

explanation.surface: Someone notes the good thing about an arrogant swimmer is that they have dumped something.
explanation.definitionFit: A guppy is a small tropical freshwater fish, popular in aquariums, so a swimmer.

clue.text: See 24
Each slow song, similarly endless, uplifting with increased speed

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting up means the letters are read from bottom to top, backwards
both words lose their final letter, the second in the same way as the first

parts.note: every means each
a ballad is a slow, sentimental song

explanation.surface: A music critic describes a set of slow songs, each building to an uplifting faster finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'similarly endless' trims both EVERY and BALLAD to EVER and BALLA; 'uplifting' then reverses EVERBALLA. Strictly, alla breve is a time signature (two minims to a bar), which makes music feel quicker.
explanation.definitionFit: Alla breve is a musical direction for cut time, counted in two, so played effectively faster.

clue.text: Refuse cars from '66 and '86?

definitions.meaning: rubbish, the sediment left at the bottom
British number plates carried a year letter; D was used for cars registered in 1966 and again in 1986, so these are D-registrations

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about turning away cars of two particular vintages.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as D-REGS: British cars registered in 1966 (suffix) and 1986 (prefix) both had a D year letter on their plates. 'Refuse' is the noun, rubbish, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Dregs are the worthless residue at the bottom of a container, so refuse or waste.

clue.text: Travelling in front, hero advances

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A war story: out in front, the hero advances.
explanation.definitionFit: To be on the road is to be on a journey or touring, that is, travelling.

clue.text: Minute remaining, matron!

parts.note: other means the rest, the remaining

explanation.surface: A hospital patient pleads for one more minute with the ward matron.
explanation.definitionFit: A matron is a married woman of dignity, often a mother; also the title of the head of a religious house.

clue.text: A lot in dancing join at the back

indicators.note: the letters of a lot in move about as if dancing, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: An invitation: plenty of people are dancing, so join in at the back.
explanation.definitionFit: To tail on is to attach oneself at the rear of a line or procession.

clue.text: What courage aunt shows with regular donation … of this?

definitions.text: What courage aunt shows with regular donation … of this?

indicators.note: taking every other letter of courage aunt, at regular intervals

explanation.surface: A tribute to an aunt brave enough to donate regularly, asking what she gives.
explanation.walkthrough: The even letters of cOuRaGe AuNt spell the answer, and the whole clue describes a brave aunt agreeing to organ donation.
explanation.definitionFit: An organ is a body part such as a kidney, which a living donor may give.

clue.text: Most scared-looking soldiers hiding a training-ground

indicators.note: the outer letters conceal the letter a within them

parts.note: palest means whitest with fear
RA is the Royal Artillery, a British army regiment

explanation.surface: Terrified soldiers concealing something at their training camp.
explanation.definitionFit: A palaestra was an ancient Greek wrestling school, a place for athletic training.

clue.text: Part-time screw grass has got in awful flap

definitions.note: screw is old slang for wages, so reduced pay for reduced hours

indicators.note: the dried grass takes the rearranged letters inside it

parts.note: hay is dried grass

indicators.note: the letters of flap are made a mess of, so rearranged

explanation.surface: A prison story: a part-time warder (a 'screw') getting into a flap over drugs smuggled in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screw' looks like prison slang for a warder or a drug-related grass, but here it is old slang for wages. 'Grass' gives HAY, not an informer.
explanation.definitionFit: Half pay is reduced wages, as paid to someone on part-time service or reserve.

clue.text: Niff given off by one bulging man of literature

parts.note: niff is British slang for a bad smell; BO is body odour, the smell a person gives off
a swell is a bulge or swelling

explanation.surface: A smelly, portly man of letters is mocked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Niff' is British slang for a bad smell.
explanation.definitionFit: James Boswell was the eighteenth-century writer famous for his biography of Samuel Johnson.

clue.text: Without any trained oarsmen for protection, Caesar may have blown it

indicators.note: the rearranged rowers surround the short word to shield it
the letters of oarsmen are drilled into a new formation

parts.note: no means not any, as in 'no money'

explanation.surface: Rowing with no trained crew to protect him, Caesar might have blown it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blown it' looks like 'messed up', but it means blew his nose. Julius Caesar is famous for his hooked profile.
explanation.definitionFit: A Roman nose is a prominent, high-bridged nose, the kind seen on Roman busts and coins.

clue.text: Terribly undiplomatic, releasing rebellious Democrat to community

definitions.note: used as an adjective, as in community services

indicators.note: the letters of undiplomatic are terribly jumbled
the letters of the rebellious pair are set free from that pool
the Democrat and to rebel against their order, so their letters are mixed

explanation.surface: Political sniping: a tactless move, letting a rebellious Democrat loose on the community.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the letters of UNDIPLOMATIC, minus D, T and O (from D + TO, jumbled, so 'rebellious'), rearrange to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Municipal means relating to a town or local government, so serving the local community.

clue.text: Regularly I'm amused that doing gigs is captivating

indicators.note: captivating means holding captive, so the touring phrase holds the chuckle inside

parts.note: a band doing gigs is on tour
heh is a small chuckle of amusement

explanation.surface: A fan says, amused, that the band's touring is enthralling.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done on the hour happens at each full hour, at regular intervals.

clue.text: See 19
Champion boxers, perhaps when cycling, suddenly halt

indicators.note: the letters go round a cycle, the last moving to the front

parts.note: top means best, champion
boxer shorts are one kind of shorts

explanation.surface: Top boxers out cycling may slam on the brakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxers' are not fighters but underpants; 'cycling' is not bike riding but moving the final S of TOPSHORTS to the start.
explanation.definitionFit: To stop short is to come to an abrupt standstill.

clue.text: Sweet cicely leaves, when drawn

wordplay.reading: CICELY drawn leaves its first, conjoined to its last

parts.note: cicely drawn, that is with its insides pulled out as a cook draws a fowl, keeps only its two outer letters

explanation.surface: Sweet cicely is a herb; this sounds like a note on its leaves once picked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet cicely' looks like one phrase (a herb), but 'Sweet' is the definition. 'Drawn' means gutted, as a chicken is drawn; emptied, CICELY leaves C AND Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Candy is the American word for sweets or confectionery.

clue.text: E.g. Putin's token record for rolling in the hay

indicators.note: the turned record is set within the pile of hay

parts.note: a cock is a small conical heap of hay, a haycock

indicators.note: the record rolls over, so its letters are read backwards

parts.note: EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A sly line about a record of the Russian president's tryst in the hay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the hay' suggests a romp, but a cock here is a haystack, a small conical heap of hay in a field.
explanation.definitionFit: A copeck is a Russian coin, a hundredth of a rouble, so the sort of small money Putin handles.

clue.text: Name scratched from Open, one shot down, could get this?

definitions.text: Name scratched from Open, one shot down, could get this?

indicators.note: the remaining letters could be rearranged into the answer
the abbreviation is struck out of the word, as a competitor is scratched

explanation.surface: A golfer withdrawn from the Open after one bad shot might win the booby prize.
explanation.walkthrough: Take N from OPEN, add ONE SHOT DOWN and rearrange. The whole clue also describes the answer: a player knocked out could end up last.
explanation.definitionFit: The wooden spoon is the mock prize given to whoever finishes last in a competition.

clue.text: 'Century, ten inferior' about nails it

indicators.note: the letters are turned about, read backwards
the phrase holds the answer pinned within it

explanation.surface: A sum checked aloud: a hundred less ten gets it exactly right.
explanation.walkthrough: Read backwards within centurY TEN INferior. The whole clue also defines: a century less ten is the number.
explanation.definitionFit: A century is a hundred, and ten fewer than a hundred is the number ninety.

clue.text: Whiter than white, it drifts in with cold snap

indicators.note: the group drifts into the middle of the word for whiter than white

parts.note: pure means spotless, beyond reproach

indicators.note: with here means holding, so the two letters hold the abbreviation

explanation.surface: A wintry scene: pure white snow drifting in during a cold snap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cold snap' looks like one phrase; 'snap' alone is the definition, a photo.
explanation.definitionFit: A snap is a snapshot, a photograph, which is one kind of image.

clue.text: In finales from Rameau to Flotow, lead violin may make this

indicators.note: the metal symbol is placed within the three letters
the last letters of the composers' names and the little word between them

parts.note: Pb is the chemical symbol for lead

explanation.surface: Music notes: in the closing bars of works by Rameau and Flotow, the lead violin plays this.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead violin' looks like the principal player, but 'lead' gives PB. Rameau and Flotow are French and German opera composers.
explanation.definitionFit: An upbow is a stroke of the violin bow pushed from tip to heel, which a violinist makes.

clue.text: Refrain from Carmen keeping our time now

indicators.note: the motoring men keep the time abbreviation between them

parts.note: read as car men: the AA, the Automobile Association, Britain's roadside rescue service
BST is British Summer Time, the setter's local clock
in means fashionable, of the moment

explanation.surface: An opera note: a refrain from Carmen, keeping time for today's audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refrain' and 'Carmen' suggest a tune from Bizet's opera, but 'Carmen' splits into car men, the AA.
explanation.definitionFit: To abstain is to hold back from doing something, so to refrain, as from voting.

clue.text: For this storyteller, the tide's turning on theatre work

indicators.note: in a down clue the word is turned round, read upwards

parts.note: the sea is where the tide runs, taken as a stand-in
op is short for opus, a work, here in the theatre

explanation.surface: A storyteller marks the turn of the tide with a seaside show.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop was the ancient Greek teller of fables, such as the tortoise and the hare.

clue.text: Cryptographic couple vexed an old cabbie

indicators.note: the letters of an old cabbie are agitated into a new order

explanation.surface: A pair of code-makers have annoyed an elderly taxi driver.
explanation.definitionFit: Alice and Bob are the stock placeholder names for sender and receiver in cryptography examples.

clue.text: Models of perfection Spock set out pricked by McCoy's latest disapproving reaction

indicators.note: the rearranged name is pierced, as by a needle, and the letters go inside
the letters of Spock are laid out afresh

parts.note: the final letter of McCoy
boo is a jeer of disapproval

explanation.surface: A Star Trek scene: Spock lays out models of perfection and Dr McCoy jeers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pricked by' fits Bones McCoy the doctor, wielding a needle; it puts Y and BOO inside COPKS, the letters of Spock set out.
explanation.definitionFit: Copybooks held perfect handwriting for pupils to copy, so exemplars, as in 'copybook manners'.

clue.text: Half the ground covered by old poet

indicators.note: by here means next to, so the half word sits beside the abbreviation for old
the first half of the word is taken

parts.note: the distance is the ground covered on a journey

explanation.surface: A rambler's note: halfway, the old poet is overtaken.
explanation.definitionFit: An odist is a poet who writes odes, lyrical verses addressed to a subject.

clue.text: Briefly fluid, I must repay Blossom

parts.note: fl is a short form of fluid
an ower is someone who owes and must repay

explanation.surface: A debtor briefly flustered, vowing to repay someone called Blossom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blossom' looks like a name to be repaid, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A blossom is a flower, especially on a fruit tree.

clue.text: 'Not quite empty!': no work for them

definitions.text: 'Not quite empty!': no work for them

indicators.note: the letters are worked into a new order
the last letter of empty is dropped, leaving it not quite complete

explanation.surface: Pub regulars warn that their glasses are not yet empty, so no clearing for the staff.
explanation.walkthrough: EMPT plus NO, rearranged. Potmen are pub workers who gather empty glasses, so a 'not quite empty' cry means no work for them.
explanation.definitionFit: Potmen are pub staff who collect and wash pots and glasses, called potboys in older use.
